title: Gulf Countries Welcome US-Iran Deal After War
summary:
Six countries in the Gulf region—Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman—are welcoming a new agreement between the United States and Iran. These countries didn't want the war between Israel and Iran that started in February. When Iran attacked Gulf cities in response to Israeli and US strikes, it made them even more eager for peace.

Now, the Gulf states are supporting diplomacy (talking instead of fighting). They want a deal that stops the war and also addresses their concerns about Iran's drones and proxies (armed groups that Iran supports). A researcher named Farah al-Qawasmi said the Gulf states want to prevent more conflicts.

Qatar is acting as a mediator (a go-between) in the talks. The Gulf states have more influence this time than in 2015, when a similar nuclear deal was made. They want an agreement that covers not just nuclear weapons but also Iran's other activities in the region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited the Gulf to reassure them that the deal won't make Iran too powerful. The Gulf states are being pragmatic (practical) — they prefer peace even if they don't fully trust Iran.
why_it_matters: Peace between countries can keep people living safely and affect the prices of things like gas that your family might use every day.

keywords.explanation: Solving problems between countries by talking instead of using military force.
Unmanned aircraft that can be used to spy or drop bombs without a pilot on board.
Armed groups that another country supports to fight on its behalf.
A person or country that helps two sides reach an agreement by talking with both.
Being practical and focusing on what works, rather than on perfect ideals.
An agreement between countries to limit the ability to build nuclear weapons.

background_read: The Gulf region sits on some of the world's largest oil reserves and has long been worried about conflict with Iran, a powerful neighbor.
In 2015, world powers made a deal (the JCPOA) to limit Iran's nuclear program, but the U.S. left that deal in 2018, raising tensions.
The war between Israel and Iran that started in February saw missiles launched at Gulf cities, making nearby countries very nervous.
Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State (America's top official for dealing with other countries), traveled there to calm fears.
Article_Structure: WHO: Six Gulf countries (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman), the United States, and Iran.
WHAT: The Gulf countries welcome a new U.S.-Iran agreement and support diplomacy to end the war.
WHERE: The Gulf region, involving talks with the U.S. and Iran.
WHY: They want to stop the war that threatened their cities and seek a deal that addresses Iran's drones and proxies, not just nuclear weapons.

perspectives.description: Feels that diplomacy brings safety and stability, protecting Gulf cities and families from attacks.
Worries that Iran will use the deal to grow stronger through proxies and might not keep its promises.
Believes that talking and finding practical solutions is better than war, even if you don't fully trust the other side.
